guide.title: Battery Park City, Manhattan: A Neighborhood Built From Landfill
guide.intro: Battery Park City takes its name from The Battery, the historic waterfront park directly to its south — but the neighborhood itself is entirely man-made. Built in the 1970s on Hudson River landfill, it was formed from more than 3 million cubic yards of soil and rock excavated during construction of the original World Trade Center, plus sand dredged from New York Harbor and stone from Water Tunnel #3; the landfill was complete by 1976. New York State created the Battery Park City Authority in 1968 to redevelop the area's deteriorated piers, but the neighborhood didn't take its current shape until a 1979 master plan by Alexander Cooper and Stanton Eckstut set the street grid, esplanade, and mixed-use form still in place today — a plan widely studied as a model of waterfront urban design. The Authority, now named for Hugh L. Carey, still governs the neighborhood.

sections.heading: Memory on the Waterfront
sections.body: Two of the neighborhood's landmarks turn its planned streets into places of memory. The Irish Hunger Memorial, dedicated July 16, 2002, incorporates an authentic 19th-century stone cottage transported from County Mayo along with stones and soil from Ireland's western coast, commemorating the Great Hunger of 1845-1852 and the more than 900,000 Irish emigrants who arrived at the port of New York in the following decade. The Museum of Jewish Heritage — A Living Memorial to the Holocaust opened September 15, 1997 in a six-sided Kevin Roche-designed building whose pyramid roof symbolizes both the Star of David's six points and the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust; its redesigned core exhibition, with interactive survivor interviews, reopened in June 2022.

sections.heading: Getting there by subway
sections.body: There is no subway station inside Battery Park City itself. Riders cross West Street via pedestrian bridges, crosswalks, or the West Concourse tunnel from Brookfield Place to reach the World Trade Center-area stations: the Chambers Street-World Trade Center/Park Place complex (A/C/E, 1/2/3), Cortlandt Street (R/W), WTC Cortlandt (1), the Fulton Street complex, and the World Trade Center PATH station.

sections.heading: Where to stay
sections.body: The Conrad New York Downtown, at 102 North End Avenue, is the neighborhood's flagship hotel — a contemporary all-suite property with a rooftop bar looking out over the Statue of Liberty and the harbor.

faq.question: How do I get to Battery Park City by subway?
faq.answer: Battery Park City has no subway station of its own. Walk across West Street (via pedestrian bridges, crosswalks, or the West Concourse tunnel from Brookfield Place) to the World Trade Center-area stations: A/C/E and 1/2/3 at Chambers Street-World Trade Center/Park Place, R/W at Cortlandt Street, 1 at WTC Cortlandt, or the Fulton Street complex.

faq.question: Is there a subway station in Battery Park City itself?
faq.answer: No — the neighborhood has no subway access of its own. The nearest stations are all across West Street in the adjoining Financial District/World Trade Center area.

faq.question: What is the Irish Hunger Memorial?
faq.answer: Dedicated July 16, 2002, it's a memorial landscape built around an authentic 19th-century stone cottage brought from County Mayo, with stones and soil from Ireland's west coast, commemorating the Great Hunger of 1845-1852 and the wave of Irish emigrants who arrived in New York in its aftermath.

faq.question: Is the Skyscraper Museum free to visit?
faq.answer: Yes — the museum has offered free admission to all visitors, though that offer is tied to a sponsorship window, so it's worth confirming current pricing before you go. It's open Wednesday through Saturday, noon to 6pm.

faq.question: Where can I stay in Battery Park City?
faq.answer: The Conrad New York Downtown at 102 North End Avenue is the neighborhood's verified flagship hotel, with an all-suite layout and a rooftop bar overlooking the harbor.

places.name: Brookfield Place
places.summary: A waterfront shopping, dining, and arts complex with dozens of shops, seven restaurants, a fast-casual food hall, free public art installations, and the North Cove yacht harbor on the Hudson.

places.name: Le District
places.summary: A French marketplace-and-restaurant complex inside Brookfield Place, spanning a bar and bistro, a cafe, a creperie and patisserie, a boulangerie, and a salad bar.

places.name: El Vez
places.summary: A regional Mexican restaurant known for birria tacos, house-made guacamole, and a list of more than 150 tequilas and mezcals.

places.name: P.J. Clarke's On the Hudson
places.summary: Battery Park City's waterfront outpost of the storied New York saloon brand P.J. Clarke's — whose 1884 original opened on Third Avenue — serving classic burgers and raw-bar fare.

places.name: Conrad New York Downtown
places.address: 102 North End Ave, New York, NY 10282
places.summary: A contemporary luxury all-suite hotel with 463 suites averaging over 430 square feet, a rooftop bar with Statue of Liberty and harbor views, and a 6,200-square-foot ballroom — the neighborhood's flagship hotel.
